title: The Sleepy Rabbit
subject: learning to tie a bowline at a lake dock, then teaching a younger sister
passage:
Theo had tied the same knot eleven times, and eleven times it had slid apart when Aunt Rosa tugged the rope.

"The rabbit comes up out of the hole," she said, tapping the loop he had made. "Around the tree, and back down the hole."

Theo frowned at the rope. His rabbit kept going down the wrong hole. Out on the lake, the little sailboat bumped against the dock as if it were tired of waiting.

On the twelfth try, he went slowly. Up through the loop. Around the long end of the rope. Back down. When Aunt Rosa pulled, the knot tightened and held.

"Now you can tie up the boat," she said.

That afternoon his younger sister, Mia, sat on the dock with a piece of string and a scowl. "Show me," she said.

Theo started to say, "Up, around, down," very fast, the way he said it in his head. Mia's string flopped into a tangle. He stopped. He remembered the eleven knots that had slid apart and the way Aunt Rosa had waited beside him without a single sigh.

"Okay," he said, sitting down next to her. "The rabbit lives in this hole. Go slow. It's a sleepy rabbit."

Mia giggled. On her fourth try, the knot held. She held it up like a prize, and Theo found that he was prouder of her knot than he had been of his own.

Nora and Sam had a plan for their mother's birthday, and the plan had a name: Operation Breakfast.

At 5:30 in the morning, they crept into the kitchen in their socks. Sam was in charge of toast. Nora was in charge of pancakes, because she had watched a cooking show twice.

The first pancake stuck to the pan. The second one flipped so high that it landed on top of the refrigerator. Biscuit, the dog, sat below it with great hope.

"Toast is easy," Sam whispered, and he pushed the lever down. Then he pushed it down again, to be safe.

A thin gray curl of smoke rose from the toaster. Then the smoke alarm began to shriek.

Biscuit barked. Nora dropped the spatula. Sam waved a dish towel at the ceiling as if he were signaling a ship.

Upstairs, a door opened. Their mother appeared in the kitchen doorway in her bathrobe, blinking at the haze, the batter on the floor, and the pancake on the refrigerator.

"Happy birthday!" the twins shouted.

For a moment she said nothing at all. Then she laughed so hard she had to sit down. She opened the window, rescued the pan, and made three perfect pancakes in about two minutes.

"This," she said, handing them each a plate, "is the best birthday breakfast anyone has ever made me."

"You made it," Sam pointed out.

"I know," said their mother. "That's what makes it funny."

title: A Muffled Clue
subject: a lost harmonica found inside a tuba by its muffled sound

Ten minutes before the spring concert, Ms. Alvarez's harmonica was gone.

She played it for one short solo in the middle of the second song. She always left it on the music stand beside her chair, resting on top of its little blue case. June, who played the tuba, sat in the chair right next to hers.

"It was right here during warm-ups," Ms. Alvarez said. The case was there. The harmonica was not.

The band members searched their pockets and their folders. Dev, who played trombone, checked under the risers. Lena checked the hallway.

While the others searched, June ran through her warm-up notes. They came out thick and dull, like someone humming into a pillow. She tried again. The same dull sound.

June frowned. Her tuba had sounded bright and loud an hour ago. She remembered what had happened right after warm-ups: Dev had tripped on a cable and bumped into the music stands, and everything on them had rattled and bounced.

June turned the tuba upside down over a chair cushion and gave it a gentle shake. Something slid through the curving tubes, clicked against the brass, and dropped onto the cushion.

It was the harmonica.

"It must have bounced into the bell," June said. "My tuba was trying to tell us."

Ms. Alvarez laughed and wiped the harmonica on her sleeve. "Then your tuba has earned a solo of its own."

title: Seven O'Clock, Alder Street
subject: a city street as its shops open between seven and eight in the morning

At seven the street is still a held breath.
The shutters are down, gray as closed eyes,
and the sidewalk keeps last night's rain
in every crack like a secret.

Then the first one goes up with a rattle:
the florist, hauling her steel door
toward the sky, and behind it,
buckets of tulips leaning out to look.

The tailor follows, slower, one hand
on his back, one hand on the chain.
The newsstand unfolds its wooden wings.
The cafe drags out four small tables
and sets a chair beside each one
as if expecting old friends.

By eight the street has opened
every eye it has.
It is talking now in bells and voices,
in coins, in the hiss of the coffee machine,
and nobody remembers
that an hour ago
it was quiet enough
to hear the rain still dripping
from the tailor's awning,
one drop,
one drop,
one drop.

title: Pell and the Tall Pot
subject: an invented trickster goat who tricks a proud headman into sharing water
passage:
In the hill village of Tarrow Ford, the people kept their rainwater in clay pots lined up along the lane, and every pot belonged to someone.

Pell the goat belonged to no one. She was clever, she was always thirsty, and she had learned that the quickest way to a drink was through somebody else's pride.

One dry summer, the headman of the village, a proud man named Orrin, announced that his pot would hold more water than any other. He had the potter build it twice as tall as the rest, and he set it at the top of the lane where everyone could admire it.

When the rains came, Orrin's pot filled slowly, for its mouth was as narrow as a cup. The small pots of the poorer families filled quickly and spilled over.

Pell watched this for three days. On the fourth, she trotted to Orrin's door and bleated so sadly that he came out.

"Headman," she said, "your great pot is too tall for an old goat. If I could only drink from it, I would tell every traveler that the wisest man in the hills lives in Tarrow Ford."

Orrin liked the sound of that. He tipped his giant pot so that Pell could reach it. But it was so heavy that once it began to lean, it would not stop. Over it went, and the water rushed down the lane, filling every small pot on its way.

The poorer families came out to find their pots brimming. Pell drank from all of them.

"Now," she said to Orrin, "the whole lane is your pot. Surely that is the largest pot in the hills."

[A paint counter at the back of a small hardware store. Cans line the shelves. MARCUS, sixteen, stands at the mixing machine. MS. OKAFOR, the owner, is stacking brushes.]

MARCUS: Ms. Okafor? The paint for Mrs. Dell's kitchen is done. Morning Wheat.

MS. OKAFOR: [without looking up] Good. She'll be here at four.

[MARCUS pries the lid off the can, then freezes.]

MARCUS: It's... greener than wheat.

MS. OKAFOR: [coming over and peering in] That is a field of peas.

MARCUS: I must have punched in the wrong code. Should I tell her the machine slipped?

MS. OKAFOR: [quietly] Is that what happened?

MARCUS: [after a pause] No.

MS. OKAFOR: Then don't say it.

[The bell over the door rings. MRS. DELL enters, holding a paint chip.]

MRS. DELL: Is my Morning Wheat ready? I've been dreaming about it all week.

MARCUS: [taking a breath] Mrs. Dell, I made a mistake when I mixed it. It came out green. I can mix a new batch right now, but it will take about twenty minutes.

MRS. DELL: [laughing] Green! Let me see. [She looks into the can.] Oh, my. That's the exact color of my grandmother's porch. [She studies it.] You know, I might paint the back door with this.

MS. OKAFOR: Then the green is yours at no charge. And Marcus will mix the wheat.

MRS. DELL: Twenty minutes? I'll go look at brushes. [She heads toward the aisles.]

MS. OKAFOR: [handing MARCUS a fresh can] The machine never slips, you know. People do. That's why we read every label twice.

MARCUS: [reading the label slowly, aloud] Morning... Wheat.

[He punches in the code carefully. Lights fade.]

The winter I was eleven, my grandmother taught me to fold a paper crane, and it took me nine days.

She kept a stack of square paper in a tin that had once held buttons. Every afternoon, while my parents were still at work, she set two squares on the kitchen table: one for her and one for me.

Her hands moved the way water moves, smoothly and without a pause. Mine moved like a car in traffic. I folded corners unevenly, creased the wrong side, and once tore the neck clean off.

"Again," she said, sliding me a fresh square.

I wanted her to fold it for me. I said so on the fourth day, and she shook her head. "Then it would be my crane," she said, "and you would still have empty hands."

On the ninth day, I made one that stood up. Its wings were crooked, and one side of its tail was fatter than the other, but it stood on the table on its own two points and did not fall over.

My grandmother picked it up and turned it in the light the way a jeweler looks at a stone. Then she set it on the windowsill above the sink, where she kept the things she meant to keep forever.

She has been gone for three years now. I fold cranes for my little cousins when they visit, and they tear the necks off, and I slide them fresh squares. "Again," I say, and I hear her voice when I say it. The crooked crane is still on the windowsill. My mother has never moved it.

title: Preference Recorded
subject: a talking lunchbox that reports a boy's lunch to his mother
passage:
The lunchbox was a birthday present from my aunt, who works for a company that makes "smart kitchen solutions." It was silver, it kept soup hot for nine hours, and it talked.

"Good afternoon, Kai," it said when I opened it in the cafeteria. "Today you have a turkey sandwich, carrot sticks, and an apple. Enjoy your balanced meal."

The kids at my table thought it was the best thing they had ever seen.

What I learned on the second day is that the lunchbox also reported back. At dinner, Mom set down her fork and said, "Your lunchbox says you traded your carrots for Owen's chips."

I glared at the lunchbox on the counter. It glowed a calm blue.

For a week, I tried to beat it. I hid my carrots in my backpack, and the lunchbox announced that the carrots had "left the container uneaten." I ate the apple in three bites before it could scan me, and it reported "rapid eating; consider chewing." I even covered its sensor with a napkin, and it said, quite politely, "I can still hear you, Kai."

On Friday, I tried something else. I opened the lid and spoke to it.

"Can you tell my mom I'd eat carrots if they were cooked? I don't like raw ones."

The lunchbox was silent for a moment. "Preference recorded," it said.

That night, Mom made roasted carrots with honey. I ate every one, and the lunchbox, sitting on the counter, glowed a pleased shade of green.

"Huh," Mom said, reading its screen. "It says this is the first time you've talked to it."

title: Nine Patches
subject: a girl who mends boarders' clothes during a hard winter in an invented town

The winter the shoe factory in Callow Bend closed, my mother turned our front room into a boarding house for three, and I became the girl who sewed.

It was not my plan. I was thirteen and had meant to spend that winter reading every book in the schoolhouse cupboard. But Mother cooked for the boarders from dawn until dark, and someone had to keep their clothes in one piece.

The first boarder was Mr. Haskett, a railroad clerk whose cuffs were always fraying. The second was Mrs. Bly, a schoolteacher who arrived with one good dress and a trunk full of books. The third was a young carpenter named Tomas, who tore the knees out of his trousers on his second day and on most days after.

I hated the needle at first. My stitches wandered like a lost dog. Mrs. Bly, who noticed everything, once held up a patched cuff and said kindly, "This cuff has had an adventure."

So I learned. I learned to make my stitches small and even by counting them under my breath. I learned that a patch should be cut a little larger than the hole, because cloth pulls away from a tear the way people pull away from a hurt. By February, Tomas could kneel on a roof all day, and his knees held.

In March, Mrs. Bly paid me in a way I didn't expect. She handed me a book from her trunk, and inside it was a slip of paper: Lessons, Tuesdays and Thursdays, after the mending is done.

Mother read the note twice. Then she put a hand on my shoulder and said nothing, which in our house meant yes.

The factory opened again in the spring, and the boarders left one by one. But I still have Tomas's trousers, patched in nine places, and I still count my stitches. I learned more that winter, from a sewing basket and a trunk of books, than in all my years of reading alone.

title: Now You Know
subject: a parent and child watching the northern lights in a dark field
exclusion_greps: night sky: a light-pollution poem exists; this one is about a display seen far from town
passage:
We drove out past the last farm light
and stood in a field so dark
my hand was a rumor in front of my face.

My father said, Wait.
So we waited, the cold climbing
up through our boot soles,
the stars sharp as salt on black cloth.

At first it was only a smudge,
a pale green breath along the north,
the kind of glow you might blame
on a town over the hill.

Then it stood up.

It rose in curtains, folding and refolding,
a green so alive it seemed to listen,
and a pink hem trembled at the bottom
as if the sky were deciding something.

No one spoke.
My father, who explains everything,
the pull of the tides, the reasons for rain,
stood with his hands in his pockets
and simply watched.

Later, in the warm car,
he said only, Now you know,
and I understood that he meant
there are things you learn
by standing quietly in the right place
long enough.
